items.title: Dipole moment and polarity of molecules

source_refs.note: The unnumbered topic Dipole Moment and Polarity of Molecules, printed pages 51-52 (Figures 3.5 to 3.7), with Quick Check 3.4 as the self-check.

blocks.text: In compounds such as HF, where the bonded atoms are from different elements, the electronic distribution between the atoms is uneven. Due to this reason, one atom carries partial positive and the other negative charge. A molecule with δ⁺ charge on one part and δ⁻ charge on the other part is called a dipole and such a molecule is said to have a dipole moment. It is a quantitative measurement of the polarity of a bond or a molecule. The dipole moments of diatomic molecules like HF, HCl, HBr, HI, NO, etc. are directed from the positive ends (δ⁺) to negative ends (δ⁻) as in Fig. 3.5. Dipole moment is measured in Debye unit (D). Higher dipole moment indicates high polarity in a molecule.

blocks.alt: Left: a dot picture of the electron cloud of HF, thickest between and around the two nuclei and spreading more on the fluorine side; the H nucleus and the F nucleus are marked with pink dots and labelled below. Right: a small H ball joined by a bond to a larger F ball, with a crossed arrow above them pointing from H to F, the direction of the dipole moment.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.5: Electron density in HF is higher near the F atom and the dipole moment is directed from H to F (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.5).

blocks.text: For compounds having more than two atoms, the dipole moment depends on the structure of the molecule. The dipole moment of water is 1.85 D which is directed from the end having two hydrogen atoms to the end with the oxygen atom as in the structure shown in Fig. 3.6. A linear H₂O molecule (H-O-H) would have zero dipole moment. The non-zero dipole moment value shows that water is a non-linear molecule. Experiments reveal that the water molecule has a v-shaped structure. In contrast, SO₂ has a dipole moment of 1.61 D and in opposite direction to that in water. H₂S is also a non-linear molecule as the individual bonds are polar, but they don’t cancel each other’s dipole moment and the overall molecule has some dipole moment.

blocks.alt: One row. Left: bent H2O, delta- on O, delta+ on each H; bond-moment arrows point from H to O, the resultant points up to O; P = 1.85 D. Middle: bent SO2, delta+ on S, delta- on each O; bond-moment arrows point from S to O, the resultant points down, away from S; P = 1.61 D. Right: a dome-shaped electron density map of water, red-orange at the top through yellow and green to blue below, with the printed note under it: red is the oxygen region, blue the hydrogen end, dipole from blue to red.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.6: Vector addition of individual bond moments in angular H2O and SO2 molecules (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.6).

blocks.text: However, some molecules have zero dipole moments as the symmetry in their structures causes the cancellation of the individual bond moments. For example, BeCl₂ is a linear molecule having two similar Cl atoms on both sides of the central atom at 180°. The individual Be-Cl bond moments are cancelled out as they are opposite in direction and equal in amount. Similarly, CCl₄ has four C-Cl bonds which are expected to have high polarity due to a large electronegativity difference between C and Cl atoms. The bond moments associated to the four C-Cl bonds are directed in such a way that they cancel each other. The net dipole moment of the CCl₄ molecule is zero making it a non-polar molecule. The CCl₄ molecule is perfectly tetrahedral. Similarly, BF₃ has a trigonal planar symmetrical structure and its dipole moment is also zero. As a rule, the molecules that have same ligands (atoms or groups of atoms with the central atom) in a regular geometry, the individual dipole moments may not be zero, but overall molecule has zero dipole moment. Such a molecule is said to be non-polar.

blocks.alt: Three symmetrical molecules, each with p = 0 D beneath it. BeCl2 is linear, Cl-Be-Cl, with a 180 degree arc. BF3 is trigonal with delta+ on B, delta- on each F and a bond-moment arrow beside each B-F bond pointing to F. CCl4 is drawn as a tetrahedral sketch with delta+ on C, delta- on each Cl and a bond-moment arrow beside each C-Cl bond pointing to Cl. The moments cancel.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.7: The individual bond moments in symmetrical molecules BeCl2, BF3 and CCl4 cancel out to give zero net dipole moment (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.7).

blocks.prompt: a) Can you explain why CO has a dipole moment but CO₂ does not have any?
blocks.explanation: CO is a molecule of two different atoms; its single bond is polar, so the molecule is a dipole. CO₂ is linear (O=C=O): its two polar C=O bond moments are equal and opposite and cancel, so its net dipole moment is zero.

blocks.prompt: b) Do you think that individual bonds in CCl₄ are polar? Explain in terms of the electronegativity difference. What about the polarity of overall CCl₄ molecule?
blocks.explanation: Yes, each C–Cl bond is polar because chlorine is considerably more electronegative than carbon. But the four bonds point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron and their moments cancel, so the CCl₄ molecule as a whole is non-polar.

blocks.prompt: c) Are these molecules polar or non-polar? Briefly give reasons. HF, CH₂Cl₂, O₂, H₂S
blocks.explanation: HF: polar (two different atoms). CH₂Cl₂: polar (C carries two H and two Cl; the bond moments are unequal and do not cancel). O₂: non-polar (two identical atoms). H₂S: polar (a bent molecule; the bond moments do not cancel).
